← NeuroAtlas XR

STAGE prenatal expression layer

NeuroAtlas links a public spatial transcriptomics dataset to an educational brain viewer. The measurements come from developing forebrain tissue. The adult brain is an anatomical reference, not a reconstruction of those developing specimens.

Primary evidence

STAGE — Spatiotemporal Gene Expression Atlas of Autism and the Sanger WebAtlas viewer provide the source dataset. Aivazidis, Memi, Rademaker and colleagues describe the work in A spatial transcriptomic atlas of autism-associated genes identifies convergence in the developing human thalamus, a 2025 preprint, DOI 10.1101/2025.11.05.685843.

The study profiled 13 coronal forebrain sections from six individuals at 16–21 gestational weeks. Its targeted panel has 310 genes: 250 autism-susceptibility genes and 65 cell-type marker genes, with five overlapping. This layer includes the 250 susceptibility genes identified in Supplementary Table S1. It does not claim to include every possible autism-associated gene. It is not an autism-versus-control contrast, a causal model, or a diagnostic map.

What the numbers mean

For each public AnnData Zarr section, we read the X raw transcript-count matrix and the paired obs/anatomical_annotation labels. We retain regional cell denominators, transcript totals and counts of cells containing at least one transcript for each susceptibility gene. Five appended NMF factor columns and marker-only genes are excluded. Published gene symbols are preserved; old array symbols H3F3A, C16orf72 and C5orf49 are matched to H3-3A, HAPSTR1 and CFAP90 respectively.

Sections are pooled within each individual and region. Individual regional means are then averaged with equal weight, so an individual with more sections does not automatically dominate. “Counts / cell” is this donor-balanced mean, not nTPM, a normalized expression score, protein abundance, or a comparison with the previous HPA layer. The percentage of positive cells is also averaged across individuals.

A region’s detected-gene list includes every panel susceptibility gene with at least one observed transcript in a segmented cell in that region. Very low counts can include background. Detection does not establish functional activity or biological importance. Zero observations do not prove biological absence. Unassigned cells are excluded from named regional lists; missing regions remain missing rather than receiving invented zero values.

How highlights are selected

DisplayExplicit descriptive rule
Regional peakEvaluate regions with at least 100 cells and two individuals. The highest donor-balanced mean must be at least 0.05 counts/cell. Highlight all qualifying regions within 80% of that peak.
Broad distributionAt least 20 eligible regions; coefficient of variation ≤0.30; the 10th-percentile regional mean ≥50% of the 90th-percentile mean; and at least 1% positive cells in at least 90% of eligible regions.
Insufficient signalNo qualifying regional peak. Low signal and absence of an enriched NMF factor are never treated as proof of uniform expression.

These are transparent interface rules, not criteria supplied or validated by the STAGE authors and not statistical tests of enrichment. Changing thresholds could change the highlights. Age, region-specific cell composition, sample coverage and technical differences can affect raw means. Highest observed expression is not an exclusive location or proof of where a gene “acts.” Broad expression among sampled forebrain regions cannot establish uniformity across the entire brain; unmeasured areas remain unknown.

Anatomy and spatial limitations

STAGE anatomical names are linked to adult reference surfaces using a curated correspondence. A prenatal frontal cortical-plate sample can supply broad frontal context, but it does not provide a separate measurement for each adult DKT gyrus. Left and right reference surfaces display the same source summary. There is no pointwise registration between STAGE tissue, BigBrain and the Harvard–Oxford atlas.

Transient prenatal compartments such as germinal zones and subplate have no matching adult surface. Their broad cortical territory may be shown for orientation, with the limitation stated in the viewer. Where available, the measured-tissue view shows actual section coordinates and anatomical annotations, reduced to a grid by majority label. It is a two-dimensional annotation map, not a three-dimensional fetal reconstruction, and its colored areas represent regional summaries rather than individually localized protein molecules.

The BigBrain cortex uses the DKT labels on a surface registered to ICBM152 2009b symmetric space. Deep surfaces derive from the Harvard–Oxford adult subcortical atlas, maximum-probability threshold 25%, 2 mm, in MNI152 space. Its label masks are converted to meshes with conservative surface smoothing. They are independent adult references; their placement is approximate relative to the BigBrain template. No new thalamic-nucleus boundaries are invented.

Protein models

The current library contains 20 independent protein models; 17 genes overlap the STAGE susceptibility panel. CNTNAP2, MET and NLGN3 remain accessible through the protein-model filter but receive no STAGE regional highlight. Most of the 250 genes have no supplied model, and the interface says so. Gene-level RNA does not identify protein abundance, splice isoform, cellular compartment or the position of an independent structure. Partial structures and AlphaFold uncertainty remain labeled.

Downloads and reproducibility

All gene-by-region summaries (CSV) · Complete evidence, donor summaries, rules and correspondence (JSON) · Downsampled source-section annotations (JSON).

The saved project source includes the supplementary panel, per-section sufficient statistics, SHA-256 checksums for downloaded expression blocks, and scripts to fetch and rebuild the layer. All 13 sections are required for a release build. The source-section cell counts and regional totals in the downloads describe the actual public viewer arrays; preprocessing and unassigned-cell inclusion may differ from totals in manuscript analyses.
